title: A guide is not a chatbot
statement: Don't build help or independent work on a text as a chat thread: independent practice should produce the learner's own writing in a structured frame, not conversation turns.
example: The chat pattern had been raised 4 times across two units when the review made replacing it a standing requirement.
detail: The review of a Grade 9 lesson prototype met the chat pattern for the fourth time across two units, this time in independent practice, where the student should be writing alone (`g9/library/text/L36b8ba.txt`, line 34), and made a guide that is not a chatbot a standing requirement (line 36). Its build checklist replaces the chat thread and turns the guide's redirect copy into per-row hints, available on request, inside the stem grid (lines 123-124). Notes from a meeting the next day record dropping the chat-based approach after feedback that it failed to support learning (`g9/library/text/L64fb8b.txt`, line 15).
against: Whether a guide replying in prose still counts as chat was left open: "whether an instructor figure replying in prose satisfies the "peer, pal, instructor" requirement, given that the chat pattern was rejected." (`g9/library/text/L36b8ba.txt`, line 378). A build meeting described what the chat was for: "So in some cases u the student answers something and then he will ask a follow-up question to probe further and through that they basically deepen their knowledge or add perspectives to their own thought." (`g9/sources/meeting-notes/Incept Service CoE Catchup - 2026_10_07 10_30 CEST - Notes by Gemini.md`, line 310). The record `dialogue-and-refutation-beat-exposition` prefers explaining through dialogue where there is time; that concerns explanation, not the learner's own work on a text.

evidence.quote: The guide is a peer, a pal, an instructor — not a chatbot. Typing an answer into a conversation and receiving a reply is the wrong model of what a child is doing when they study a text, and it is the wrong message about where answers come from.
